title: Async pitfalls
summary: The mistakes everyone makes once: async void, forgotten awaits, blocking on tasks, and Task.Run in the wrong place.

steps.title: async void
body: An async method can be declared to return `void`. It compiles. It is almost always a mistake.
```csharp fragment
static async void SaveAsync(Order order)    // bad
static async Task SaveAsync(Order order)    // good
With `async void` the caller gets **no task back**. That means:
- The caller **cannot await it**. It has no way to know when the save is finished.
- The caller **cannot catch its exceptions**. There is no task to carry them, so an exception inside an `async void` method typically crashes the whole process.
The fix is always the same: return `Task` instead of `void`.
`async void` exists for one case only: event handlers in UI frameworks, such as a button's click handler, whose signature must return `void`.

steps.prompt: Why is `static async void SendEmailAsync(string to)` a problem?
options: The caller cannot await it or catch its exceptions
It runs more slowly than `async Task`
It blocks the calling thread until the email is sent
steps.explain: It can use `await` and it does not block. The trouble is on the caller's side: with no `Task` returned, there is nothing to await and nowhere for an exception to go.

steps.title: The forgotten await
body: Calling an async method without `await` still **starts** it. You just do not wait for it.
```csharp fragment
static async Task CheckoutAsync(Order order)
SaveAsync(order);                 // oops: no await
Console.WriteLine("Saved!");      // printed before the save has finished
This is called **fire and forget**, and it is rarely what you want:
- The code after it runs too early.
- If `SaveAsync` fails, nobody sees the exception. The order is silently not saved.
- The program can even exit while the save is still in progress.
The compiler helps: inside an async method it gives warning **CS4014**, "this call is not awaited". Treat that warning as an error.
If the method returns a value you usually notice at once, because a `Task<int>` will not fit in an `int`. The dangerous ones are the methods that return a plain `Task`.

steps.explain: `SaveAsync()` starts and returns a task as soon as it reaches the delay. Nothing awaits that task, so the program carries straight on, prints, and ends 2 seconds before `saved` would have been added.

steps.title: Blocking on a task
body: A task has members that force the answer out of it **without** `await`:
```csharp fragment
int stock = GetStockAsync("TEA").Result;                 // blocks
SaveAsync(order).Wait();                                 // blocks
int stock2 = GetStockAsync("TEA").GetAwaiter().GetResult();   // blocks
They are tempting, because the calling method then does not need to be `async`. Do not use them. This is called **sync over async**:
- The thread is **blocked** for the whole wait. That is exactly what async exists to avoid.
- In UI apps and some server frameworks it can **deadlock**: the blocked thread is the one the task needs in order to finish, so both wait for ever.
- `.Result` and `.Wait()` wrap failures in an `AggregateException`, so your `catch` for the real exception type no longer matches.
The answer is the rule from the first lesson: **async all the way**. Make the caller `async` and `await`.
(Reading `.Result` of a task you have *already awaited* is harmless: it is finished. But `await` works there too, so just use `await`.)

steps.explain: The three pitfalls so far: `async void` (nothing to await), a missing `await` (work and errors are lost), and `.Result` / `.Wait()` (a blocked thread).

steps.title: Code review
prompt: The tests provide `Prices.GetAsync(int id)`, which returns a `Task<int>`.

`TotalAsync` adds up the prices of some products, writes a line such as `total 60` to the log, and returns the total. It was written in a hurry and has **three** async mistakes, one of each kind you have just seen.
When `await TotalAsync(ids, log)` has finished, the log line must already be in `log`.
starter: static async void LogAsync(List<string> log, string message)
await Task.Delay(300);   // the audit log sits on a slow disk
static async Task<int> TotalAsync(List<int> ids, List<string> log)
solution: static async Task LogAsync(List<string> log, string message)
await Task.Delay(300);   // the audit log sits on a slow disk
static async Task<int> TotalAsync(List<int> ids, List<string> log)
template: int total = await TotalAsync(new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 }, log);
Dojo.Eq("the log line is written before TotalAsync finishes", "total 60", logged);
public static async Task<int> GetAsync(int id)
hints: Mistake 1 is in the first line: `LogAsync` returns `void`, so nobody can wait for it. Make it return `Task`.
Mistake 2: `.Result` blocks the thread. Replace it with `await` in front of the call: `total += await Prices.GetAsync(id);`
Mistake 3: `LogAsync(...)` is called but not awaited, so `TotalAsync` returns before the line is logged. Put `await` in front of it.

steps.title: Task.Run is for CPU work
body: There are two reasons code can take a long time, and they need different tools.
**Waiting on I/O** (database, HTTP, files): nothing in your program is busy. Use the async method and `await` it. No extra thread is needed.
```csharp fragment
string json = await client.GetStringAsync(url);

**CPU-bound work** (resizing images, crunching a big report, hashing): the processor really is busy, and there is no async version to call. `Task.Run` moves that work to a background thread and gives you a task to await:
```csharp fragment
int primes = await Task.Run(() => CountPrimes(5_000_000));
That keeps a desktop app responsive while the calculation runs.
The common mistake is to wrap I/O in `Task.Run`:
```csharp fragment
var json = await Task.Run(() => client.GetStringAsync(url));   // pointless

That borrows a thread only to start something that needs no thread. And `Task.Run` around a *blocking* call, such as `Task.Run(() => File.ReadAllText(path))`, just moves the blocked thread somewhere else. Call the async version instead: `File.ReadAllTextAsync(path)`.

steps.prompt: Which line is a good use of `Task.Run`?
options: `var thumbnail = await Task.Run(() => ResizeImage(photo));` where `ResizeImage` is a slow, ordinary method
steps.explain: Resizing an image keeps the CPU busy and has no async version, so a background thread is the right tool. The others are already async I/O: await them directly. The last one also blocks with `.Result`.

steps.title: Two more types you will meet
body: **`ValueTask<T>`** is a lighter alternative to `Task<T>`. Libraries use it for methods that usually have the answer ready *without* waiting, such as a cache lookup, because it avoids creating a task object each time. You use it the same way: `await` it, once. For your own methods, `Task<T>` is the right default.

**`IAsyncEnumerable<T>`** is the async version of `IEnumerable<T>`: a sequence whose items **arrive over time**, such as pages from an API or rows streaming from a database. You write one with `async` plus `yield return`, and you read one with **`await foreach`**:
```csharp fragment
static async IAsyncEnumerable<Order> ReadOrdersAsync()
for (int page = 1; page <= 3; page++)
List<Order> orders = await LoadPageAsync(page);   // wait for a page
foreach (Order order in orders)
yield return order;                            // hand its items out
await foreach (Order order in ReadOrdersAsync())
Console.WriteLine(order.Id);
It is lazy, just like an iterator: page 2 is only loaded when the loop gets that far. If the loop stops early, the remaining pages are never requested.

steps.prompt: Match each situation to the right tool.
pairs: Compress a large file in memory
A click handler in a desktop app
Read rows as they stream in from a server
A library method that usually answers from a cache

steps.title: Import your GitHub issues
prompt: **Sidekick piece: `sk import owner/repo`.** Your Sidekick turns the open issues of a GitHub repository into tasks. GitHub sends issues in **pages**; the template asks for one page at a time over `HttpClient`, and your code decides when to ask for the next.
The tests give you `AddRequest` (your record from Robust code). Write the two records and two methods:
record Issue(int Number, string Title, string[] Labels);

1. `static async IAsyncEnumerable<Issue> AllIssues(Func<int, Task<IssuePage>> fetchPage)`: ask for page 1, 2, 3, ... and yield every issue in order. Stop after a page whose `HasMore` is `false`, or that has no items. It must be **lazy**: a page is only fetched when the reader wants an issue from it.

2. `static async Task<List<AddRequest>> ImportRequests(IAsyncEnumerable<Issue> issues, int max)`: read with `await foreach` and turn each issue into `new AddRequest($"#{Number} {Title}", firstLabelOrNull, null, 0)`. Stop as soon as you have `max` requests.
// [ AddRequest("#12 Login loops", "bug", null, 0), AddRequest("#15 Docs typo", null, null, 0) ]   page 2 never fetched
Write the methods first and the two records at the bottom.
starter: static async IAsyncEnumerable<Issue> AllIssues(Func<int, Task<IssuePage>> fetchPage)
static async Task<List<AddRequest>> ImportRequests(IAsyncEnumerable<Issue> issues, int max)
record Issue(int Number, string Title, string[] Labels);
solution: static async IAsyncEnumerable<Issue> AllIssues(Func<int, Task<IssuePage>> fetchPage)
static async Task<List<AddRequest>> ImportRequests(IAsyncEnumerable<Issue> issues, int max)
record Issue(int Number, string Title, string[] Labels);
template: 1 => new IssuePage(new List<Issue> { new(12, "Login loops", new[] { "bug", "auth" }), new(15, "Docs typo", new string[0]), new(16, "Dark mode", new[] { "feature" }) }, true),
2 => new IssuePage(new List<Issue> { new(20, "Slow search", new[] { "perf" }), new(21, "Crash on save", new[] { "bug" }) }, true),
_ => new IssuePage(new List<Issue> { new(30, "Last one", new string[0]) }, false),
await foreach (var issue in AllIssues(DojoFetch)) dojoAll.Add(issue.Number);
Dojo.Eq("AllIssues yields every issue of every page, in order", new List<int> { 12, 15, 16, 20, 21, 30 }, dojoAll);
Dojo.Eq("and stops after the page that says there are no more", new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 }, dojoPages);
Dojo.Eq("it is lazy: two issues need only page 1", new List<int> { 1 }, dojoPages);
Dojo.Eq("a request is titled #number title, tagged with the first label", new AddRequest("#12 Login loops", "bug", null, 0), dojoFirst[0]);
Dojo.Eq("an issue with no labels has no tag", new AddRequest("#15 Docs typo", null, null, 0), dojoFirst[1]);
Dojo.Eq("pages asked for max 4", new List<int> { 1, 2 }, dojoPages);
await foreach (var issue in AllIssues(async p => { await Task.Delay(1); dojoEmpty.Add(p); return new IssuePage(new List<Issue>(), true); })) dojoEmpty.Add(-1);
Dojo.Eq("an empty page ends the stream even if it says there are more", new List<int> { 1 }, dojoEmpty);
record AddRequest(string Title, string? Tag, string? Project, int EstimateMinutes);

require.message: Yields issues one at a time
Reads the stream with await foreach

forbid.message: Does not read the whole stream up front

hints: `for (int page = 1; ; page++)`: fetch, `foreach (var issue in result.Items) yield return issue;`, then `if (!result.HasMore || result.Items.Count == 0) yield break;`.
In `ImportRequests`, check `if (requests.Count == max) break;` at the top of the `await foreach` body.
steps.explain: Because the stream is lazy, `sk import` with a limit of 50 never downloads page 3 of a repository with 1,000 issues. `await foreach` plus `yield return` is the async version of the deferred execution you met with LINQ.
